title_en: Comac ends C919 delivery drought with ‘slow progress’, sources say
content_en:
Chinese planemaker has delivered first narrowbody jet since end of September, but lack of engines still a drag on production schedule.
A C919 narrowbody airliner at the Zhuhai air show in Guangdong province in 2024. Photo: Reuters
The manufacturer of China’s narrowbody C919 airliner has ended a two-month delivery drought, with sources saying it indicated the country’s leading civilian aircraft manufacturer was not “sitting on its hands” and was still making slow progress.
They added that efforts to stabilise production were continuing and might result in increased output once supply chain conditions improved.
Commercial Aircraft Corporation of China (Comac) delivered a C919 to China Eastern Airlines on Thursday evening – the first to be delivered to a carrier since the end of September – according to flight records and a tally by the South China Morning Post and aviation experts.
However, the previous production hiccups encountered by Comac have pushed its initial delivery target for the indigenous single-aisle jet this year way off course.
“Total deliveries for 2026 may be around 15, the same as last year’s and well short of Comac’s initial hopes for 28,” one source with knowledge of Comac’s production scheduling said.
Comac has delivered 44 C919s since the plane’s maiden commercial flight in May 2023, having been touted as China’s challenger to the dominant and lucrative Boeing 737 and Airbus A320 series.
The source said Comac was pressing ahead – against profound odds – with remedies designed to get production back on track.
“It is focusing on aspects it can control,” he said, adding that it had asked domestic contractors to supply parts, including wings, doors and cockpit sections, much faster so that it could speed up the assembly of C919 airframes.
Production line automation, quality control and staff training and rotation were among other aspects being further streamlined to enhance efficiency, the source said.
A photo posted on China’s Weibo microblog that is believed to have been taken last month shows some engineless C919 “gliders” sitting on the tarmac with other planes at Comac’s production base near Shanghai’s Pudong airport. Photo: Weibo
“So there is no delay in Comac’s own production,” he said. “More C919 ‘gliders’ – with their wings bare – are sitting on the tarmac [at Comac’s Shanghai plant]. They can swiftly be delivered to customers after a few trial flights once Western engines arrive.”
China Eastern was poised to receive at least one more C919 next month, he said.
On-again-off-again supplies of Leap-1C engines have been holding back Comac’s bid to spin up delivery.
The cutting-edge, high-bypass turbofan engine was developed by CFM International, a consortium formed by America’s GE Aerospace and France’s Safran.
Another source also cited engine supply as the main hold-up.
“Comac needs to seek unit-by-unit engine export approval [from the United States government], one at a time,” they said. It is not a lump sum deal … whether approval is granted, when it is granted and how many units are approved in a given year – all of these decisions remain out of its control.”
The Trump administration in Washington suspended aero engine shipments to China for a number of weeks last year, when the two countries were locked in a full-blown trade war.
A domestic replacement, the CJ-1000A engine, is being developed and tested but a wider roll-out is anything but imminent.
Comac executives have responded to the delivery snags with inspections and encouragement.
Comac chairman He Dongfeng and general manager Shen Bo have visited assembly lines, procurement centres and training facilities since the third quarter, exhorting frontline workers to remain confident, an article posted on the company’s website said.
Civil Aviation Administration of China (CAAC) director Song Zhiyong visited Comac’s headquarters in Shanghai last month, where he inspected C919 production facilities and was briefed on Comac’s production plans for the remainder of the year.
Describing the challenges it faced as “extraordinary” and commending the planemaker’s “fighting spirit”, Song pledged the industry regulator’s “full support”, according to a CAAC memo about the inspection trip seen by the SCMP.
By Frank Chen

title_en: Why southern China’s Huaqiangbei electronics hub is attracting more foreign visitors
content_en:
Daily numbers are up about 50 per cent this year, with even more flooding the area last week, when Shenzhen hosted a summit of Asia-Pacific leaders.
Neon lights glow at shops in the Huaqiangbei electronics hub in Shenzhen’s Futian district last month. Photo: Reuters
Phillip, a French tourist who recently visited the sprawling Huaqiangbei electronics market in the southern Chinese tech hub of Shenzhen, said videos of the area posted on YouTube had piqued his curiosity about its global reputation.
Huaqiangbei, often described as China’s No 1 electronics street, is one of the world’s largest electronics trading hubs, bringing together suppliers of components, consumer gadgets and emerging technologies in a densely packed commercial district.
Covering about 1.45 sq km (0.5 square miles), it is home to 35 specialised markets and more than 115,000 businesses. Its supply chain covers nearly 90 per cent of all consumer-electronics product categories, according to Shenzhen Daily.
“I’m overwhelmed,” the Frenchman said. “I just wanted to understand what this place is and what you can find and maybe catch a deal.
“But it’s amazing to see so many people interested in technology. And it’s not something that I would have been able to see in any other part of the world.”
The number of foreign visitors drawn to Huaqiangbei has been growing. It has attracted an average of more than 10,000 a day this year – up about 50 per cent year on year – according to the 21st Century Business Herald.
The influx was even greater last week, when Shenzhen hosted the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation leaders’ summit, with a daily average of 13,000 foreign visitors, the Shenzhen Special Zone Daily reported, while adding that overall visitor numbers were up 25 per cent and sales had climbed 40 per cent.
People walk past shops selling AI-powered toys in Shenzhen’s Huaqiangbei electronics market last week. Photo: Reuters
Another visitor, Jacob – an American based in Hong Kong – said he had used AI to get recommendations on what to explore in Huaqiangbei.
“I think it’s very modern and it’s impressive for such a big city,” he said. “It doesn’t feel that busy anywhere. I was actually surprised. It’s kind of quiet for how many people live here.”
“And it’s impressive just how many products there are and how many things that you won’t see in other places.”
In Huaqiangbei, he tried out “impressive” AI-augmented glasses and translation devices, but added that their prices and practicality meant further consideration was warranted before making any purchase.
Home to global technology companies such as BYD, Huawei Technologies, Tencent Holdings and DJI, Shenzhen is increasingly emerging as a destination for foreign tourists trying to experience China’s futuristic technology, from robotaxis and drone deliveries to humanoid robots and artificial intelligence-powered gadgets.
“Foreign visitors have always been quite common here, but previously most came from South Asia, the Middle East and Africa to buy goods for their businesses,” said Chen Lei, a vendor at Huaqiangbei’s SEG Electronics Market. “Since the beginning of this year, however, we have seen an increasing number of tourists from Europe and the US.
“Quite a few YouTubers come here to do live-streaming, but I think most are visiting to look around and experience the place, treating it more like a tourist attraction, because they don’t actually buy much.”
By Mia Nurmamat

title_en: Beauty defies consumers’ spending slowdown as China’s brands look to expand globally
content_en:
Shoppers are cutting back on travel and dining while spending more on beauty products and services in several countries.
A customer applies make up at a store in Beijing. Photo: AFP
As holiday shopping gets under way across the globe with Black Friday sales, beauty products and services are grabbing a bigger share of consumers’ budgets while many retail categories lose traction.
Beauty stands out as one of the few categories that have sustained growth over the past three years, according to a report by Ruder Finn Asia, Mintel and Meltwater that surveyed consumers in 15 markets across five regions, including China, the US, Britain, Singapore and Australia.
After covering essential expenses, consumers’ willingness to spend disposable income on beauty products – as well as beauty and hair services – edged up 1.1 and 0.8 percentage points, respectively, between March 2025 and March 2026, according to the report, Chinese Brands: 2027 Global Growth Outlook, which was released on Tuesday.
By contrast, consumers’ appetite for dining out, clothing, footwear and travel, as well as for savings and investments, declined. Travel posted the steepest drop, according to the report, which drew on five surveys conducted between 2024 and 2026.
“The trend of consumption upgrading is not over. It has instead narrowed to purchases that deliver tangible benefits and come with manageable one-off costs,” wrote the lead author of the report, Elan Shou, global chief growth officer and managing director of Asia and Greater China at Ruder Finn.
“As shoppers grow more prudent, brands should highlight demonstrable outcomes and comparable value.”
Florasis cosmetic products are displayed at a store in Shanghai. Photo: Reuters
A growing number of Chinese beauty makers are expanding overseas. Florasis, a Chinese beauty brand based in Hangzhou, in China’s eastern Zhejiang province, has opened a flagship store in Tokyo. It is now available on the e-commerce platform of the largest US beauty retailer, Ulta Beauty, and has entered the United Arab Emirates and other markets.
“Since we started sales on Ulta Beauty in late 2025, our business performance has been in line with expectations, and the main consumer group is local Americans. title_en: No warning, no mercy: why China moved fast to topple Chen Jining
content_en:
Abrupt detention of promising Shanghai party boss highlights Beijing’s fury over top-level wrongdoing after fifth plenum.
Many expected Chen Jining, pictured in Shanghai on January 31, to have a bright political future. Photo: Reuters
Just days after President Xi Jinping returned to Beijing from the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) leaders’ meeting and bilateral engagements in Shenzhen, the ruling Communist Party’s anti-corruption watchdog struck at the top office in China’s financial capital.
Late Tuesday, authorities announced that Chen Jining, 62, a Politburo member and Shanghai’s party chief, had been placed under investigation for suspected “serious violations of discipline and law” – standard official terminology for corruption and political misconduct.
The speed of Chen’s fall from a seemingly untouchable post is rarely seen in China’s top-level anti-corruption campaigns, and it is an unmistakable signal of Beijing’s zero-tolerance stance on high-level graft and its determination to root out senior officials, regardless of rank.
In the week before his detention, Chen made two public appearances in Shanghai, chairing an anti-graft meeting on November 17 and inspecting shipping giant Cosco on November 19.
[embedded media]
A Shanghai source familiar with the November 19 inspection said Chen again showed “his technocratic side”, breaking down the mega task of upgrading Shanghai’s status in global shipping into various steps.
These included identifying industry trends, taking stock of Shanghai’s strengths and weaknesses, asking for policy recommendations and identifying the relevant departments for follow-ups.
“All appeared normal, all was calm,” the source recalled, adding that no one around Chen could see “the slightest hint that he would be sent to the political guillotine just five days later”.
Several sources said that party and government departments across Shanghai were left stunned following the announcement of Chen’s investigation at 7.30pm Tuesday.
That night, countless officials were forced to work into the wee hours to scrub from government websites and various official materials any mentions of the city’s top boss, whose presence had been ubiquitous in Shanghai.
Another Shanghai source said on the night of Chen’s detention that a task force comprising dozens of officials from both the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection and the National Audit Office had arrived in the city, adding that they were expected to carry out extended months-long investigations.
Some said, in hindsight, that the only suggestion of anything amiss was Chen’s unexpected absence from the November 5 opening ceremony of the ninth China International Import Expo in Shanghai, where Politburo Standing Committee member and Vice-Premier Ding Xuexiang delivered the keynote speech.
But Chen soon reappeared that afternoon, joining Ding in meetings.
[embedded media]
Under the standard procedure of the party’s disciplinary apparatus, such a sweeping anti-corruption crackdown is launched once top leaders review a comprehensive report from investigators on high-ranking officials’ graft.
Rapidly and decisively detaining powerful suspects who hold critical positions is necessary, as mishandling cases involving prolonged access to top-level party and state secrets carries substantial political and security risks.
Over the past three decades, whenever a Politburo-ranked provincial leader has fallen from grace, Beijing has typically moved swiftly, detaining the official in question and their accomplices and appointing a caretaker to steady the ship, often within days.
Such was the case with the corruption scandal of Beijing party chief Chen Xitong in 1995; the investigation of Shanghai party chief Chen Liangyu in 2006; the abrupt removal of Chongqing party chief Bo Xilai at the close of the annual parliamentary session in March 2012; and the July 2017 ousting of Bo’s eventual successor, Sun Zhengcai, who had taken over from Zhang Dejiang.
By acting fast against Chen, party leaders acquired ample time – nearly a year before the 21st party congress – to manage subsequent personnel moves, including appointing an interim caretaker and eventual successor for Shanghai’s top post.
Unlike the anti-corruption blitzkrieg that swept up Chen, the handling of former Xinjiang party chief Ma Xingrui, who stepped down from his post in July last year, was marked by prolonged sidelining.
After being replaced by senior United Front official Chen Xiaojiang that July, Ma disappeared from public view that November. The absence sparked intense speculation before authorities officially placed him under investigation in April, expelled him from the party in July and indicted him on bribery charges this month.
According to China’s Supervision Law, detention may be imposed on public officials when authorities have initial findings of serious duty-related violations or crimes – such as corruption, bribery or dereliction of duty – provided they have already obtained some factual evidence and the case is major or complicated, or the suspect poses a risk of fleeing, committing suicide, colluding with others, tampering with evidence or otherwise obstructing the investigation.
[embedded media]
This gives investigators additional months to collect further evidence of corruption.
Chen’s long-established reputation as promising – given his relatively young age, English fluency, overseas degree and environment rectification track record – had fuelled expectations of his continued ascent as a strong contender for an influential role on the Politburo Standing Committee following next year’s 21st party congress.
All those expectations shattered in a one-paragraph corruption investigation statement, making his downfall all the more startling.
And there are clear political signs that the ‘Chen Jining shock’ might not end with his detention, as the party’s leadership has repeatedly warned that nobody is safe from its anti-corruption sword, regardless of their rank.
One of the latest top directives came less than a month before Chen’s detention.
At the party’s fifth plenum in late October, delegates adopted a resolution pledging to sustain “full and rigorous party self-governance” and declaring that “no one can be an ‘iron-hat prince’ or use an ‘imperial pardon warrant’”, regardless of rank, seniority or past merit.
The term iron-hat prince comes from Qing dynasty hereditary peerages whose titles passed down to descendants without reduction in rank, symbolising permanent status, entrenched power networks and untouchable seniority.
Similarly, ancient Chinese emperors often granted imperial pardon warrants to meritorious officials to exempt them from capital punishment. The practice turned past merit or royal favour into a shield against accountability.
While previously there had been a period when high-ranking officials were regarded as relatively untouchable, now Beijing has made it apparent that its disciplinary rules apply to one and all.
By William Zheng

title_en: Hackers breach US Air Force Cloud One platform, putting military data at risk
content_en:
Cloud One was launched in 2017 as a one-stop shop for the Air Force’s IT needs, including personnel data and pay, logistics and maintenance.
US Vice-President JD Vance talks to troops at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base in Ohio after serving an early Thanksgiving lunch on Wednesday. Photo: AFP
Hackers have breached the US Air Force’s flagship cloud computing platform, three people familiar with the matter said, in a development that could jeopardise a vast swathe of sensitive tactical, personnel and logistics data.
The intrusion at Cloud One was discovered within the past month or so during work to upgrade the system, two of the people said, adding that the discovery had led to disruption across the platform.
In a statement, the Air Force said it “does not comment on the security posture, vulnerabilities or operational status of specific networks and systems. We continuously take prudent measures to protect Department [of the Air Force] information, systems and mission capabilities”.
Initiated in 2017, Cloud One was meant to serve as a one-stop shop for the Air Force’s IT needs, combining the resources of four operators – Microsoft, Amazon, Oracle and Alphabet – to power scores of applications including ones that manage personnel data and pay or logistics and maintenance.
US Air Force fighter jet F-35 performs aerobatic manoeuvres on the second day of the Aero India 2023 at Yelahanka airbase in Bengaluru. Photo: AP
Among them are the Air Force’s Cloud-Based Command and Control, which collates air defence radar and other data feeds from across North America, and the Theatre Integrated Combat Munitions System, which tracks bombs and missiles across more than 200 US Air ‌Force locations around the world.
SAIC was the prime contractor for Cloud One until 2025, when Leidos took over. SAIC did not respond to a request seeking comment. Leidos referred questions to the air force.
Cloud One is among the US military’s biggest cloud platforms, according to two of ‌the sources. “A breach here is a big deal,” one of the sources said.
Investigators have called in Cyber Command, the US military’s cyber force, ⁠to assess the damage, according to one of the ⁠sources.
Cyber Command did not respond to requests for comment.
The US Air Force flies near The White House as President Donald Trump and China’s President Xi Jinping watch a military review, on September 24. Photo: AP
The discovery of the hack led to a range of disruption. Two of the sources, along with a fourth person familiar with the matter, said ‌that efforts to migrate back-office applications to Cloud One, a long-standing military priority, had been paused.
Updates to applications already running on Cloud One were blocked, leaving air force personnel unable to apply fixes just as a new batch of ‌serious software ‌vulnerabilities has been disclosed across the technology industry. A fifth source said that some users had their administrator rights revoked.
All five sources spoke on condition of anonymity.
One source said ‌that the cyber intruders exploited a software vulnerability to reach the control plane. That person likened the control plane to a universal remote, as intruders in theory could leverage their access ⁠to check the operational status of military aircraft or the movement of spare parts – though it was unclear whether the hackers did so in this case.
News of the breach comes amid heightened anxiety over AI-powered intrusions, a particularly serious problem for cloud-based networks because of the ability of AI models to swiftly detect weaknesses across wide surface areas.
The US government has already been dealing with the fallout from at least ‌six other recently disclosed cyber incidents, including two at ‌the FBI, a previous hack of Pentagon data, a recent leak of Department of Homeland Security personnel information, a breach affecting at least two spy agencies and a hack at the Treasury Department.
Cloud One has long been in the crosshairs of hackers.
In a 2023 commentary carried by the online publication FedScoop, Cloud One’s leadership touted what they called a “100 per cent success rate” in beating back what they said was a “staggering” number of attempts to penetrate the platform.
“There is no room for error when it comes to security,” Cloud One’s leadership wrote.
By Reuters

title_en: Cash-strapped AirAsia pushes back Malaysian paydays, axes 90 Philippine pilots
content_en:
Southeast Asia’s largest budget airline had previously paid Malaysian staff salaries in the second half of each month.
A staff member  stands next to a logo of AirAsia at Kuala Lumpur International Airport Terminal 2 in Sepang on September 18. Photo: Reuters
Loss-making AirAsia will temporarily delay salary payments to the end of each month, according to the airline on Friday, as it takes measures to conserve cash and its Philippine unit cuts jobs.
Confirming an earlier report, the company described the change in the payment schedule for ‌its Malaysian employees, usually paid before the end of each month, as an “operational adjustment” as it aligned internal payroll processes.
The move did not represent a change to workers’ salary entitlement, with wages to continue to be paid in full, AirAsia Chief Executive Bo Lingam said in a statement.
“We remain committed to ensuring our employees are supported throughout the process and will communicate any further changes directly to our Allstars,” Lingam said, using AirAsia’s name for its staff.
Malaysia’s government has been weighing options to support AirAsia, as a surge in fuel prices due to the Iran war has exacerbated the airline’s losses.
Reuters had ⁠reported on the salary delay earlier on Friday, citing an email sent to Malaysia-based staff late last week by Chief People Officer Muhammad Khurram Zia.
Salary payments between November ‌and March would be made on the 30th of each month or the last day of February, the email said. It cited a “challenging environment” and asked employees for “patience and flexibility”.
Ground crew work on an AirAsia plane at Kuala Lumpur International Airport Terminal 2 on January 21. Photo: Reuters
The email’s contents were confirmed by two people familiar with the matter. One ‌of the people said AirAsia, Southeast Asia’s largest budget airline, had previously paid salaries earlier in the second half of each month.
Soaring fuel prices this year have ⁠put airlines worldwide under their worst financial strain since the Covid-19 pandemic.
US low-cost carrier Spirit Airlines collapsed in May, Latvia’s airBaltic sought bankruptcy protection in September and Norway’s Norse Atlantic suspended flights on Thursday as it looks ‌for urgent short-term financing.
Shares in AirAsia, which employs about 26,000 people predominantly in Asia, have plunged more than 70 per cent this year as elevated fuel prices and foreign exchange losses squeezed its operations.
AirAsia Philippines said on Thursday it ‌would reduce ‌its workforce following sustained pressure on its operating costs, without specifying how many staff would be affected.
The airline said on Friday it remained fully operational and committed to serving ‌the Philippine market. The planned workforce adjustment would not affect passenger flights, booking or other services, AirAsia Philippines General Manager and President Anna Victoria Lu said in a statement.
The ⁠AirAsia Philippines Pilots’ Union filed notice of a strike after 90 pilots were retrenched, its president said in a video posted on social media on Thursday.
Philippine Labour Secretary Francis ⁠Tolentino confirmed receiving the notice.
AirAsia reported its third consecutive quarterly loss on Monday, though it was narrower than the prior quarter. Its cash and bank balances stood at 905 million ringgit (US$220 million) as of September 30, down 5 per cent from June 30.
In an investor presentation ‌accompanying its results, the airline said it was ‌taking measures to conserve cash, including suspending unviable routes and returning 25 planes to lessors.
It said more planes could exit its fleet in 2027, and a creditor restructuring was under way as part of a plan to reset the business before rebuilding in 2028.
Malaysia’s finance ministry said on Thursday that it would ask AirAsia for priority over other lenders and strengthen oversight of the airline’s board and management if it decided to extend support.
By Reuters

title_en: Why South Korea’s chip boom is now a US tariff trap as a US$350b pledge looms
content_en:
Analysts warn Seoul’s 15 per cent tariff rate could hit 25 per cent over chip glut claims and a US$350 billion pledge as Seoul pushes back.
Visitors view an SK Hynix display at the 28th Semiconductor Exhibition in Seoul, South Korea in October. Photo: Reuters
Washington’s latest trade investigation has created a dilemma for South Korea, forcing it to defend the state-backed industrial strategy that helped make it a semiconductor powerhouse while facing renewed pressure to shift more manufacturing capacity to the United States to deliver on investment commitments, analysts said.
They warned the move could give Washington leverage to revisit tariff terms, enforce existing investment pledges and press Seoul to commit more capital to the US.
The Office of the US Trade Representative (USTR) on Wednesday proposed new tariffs targeting 14 major trading partners – including South Korea, China, Japan and the European Union – over what it described as excess industrial capacity, following an investigation launched in March across 16 economies that left determinations on Mexico and Norway pending.
While Seoul insists the 15 per cent tariff rate agreed under its trade deal struck with Washington last year will remain in place, analysts warned it could rise to 25 per cent if South Korea failed to honour the US$350 billion investment pledge included in the agreement.
“The USTR’s Section 301 investigation report has effectively made the 15 per cent tariff rate conditional, with the possibility of an increase to 25 per cent if certain conditions are not met,” said Hur Jung, an economics professor at Sogang University.
“Allegations of semiconductor overcapacity and delays in implementing the US$350 billion investment package have emerged as major risk factors,” he said.
South Korea needed to continue convincing Washington that its industrial strategy was aimed at supply-chain cooperation rather than competition among market economies, aside from non-market economies such as China, he added.
The USTR accused South Korea of contributing to global industrial overcapacity through government-led industrial policies, preferential financing and aggressive export promotion, arguing that these practices distort market competition and undermine American manufacturing.
Its 194-page report, compiled under Section 301 of the US Trade Act of 1974, identified the automotive, semiconductor and petrochemical industries as particularly problematic. It argued that decades of industrial planning had led Seoul to pursue increasingly aggressive policies to expand manufacturing capacity while failing to adequately regulate foreign direct investment and address growing imports from non-market economies, particularly China.
Hur said the investigation had introduced a new friction point into the trade relationship.
“The issue of overcapacity is a new point of contention that was not included in the original agreement,” he said.
Shipping containers and cranes sit at Busan New Port in South Korea in August. Photo: AFP
Cho Seong-dae, director of trade policy and strategy at the Korea International Trade Association, said the report appeared primarily intended to pressure Seoul into implementing the bilateral trade and investment commitments outlined in last year’s fact sheet.
“Washington appears to be seeking justification for maintaining the existing tariff levels, rather than explicitly threatening to raise tariffs to 25 per cent,” Cho said.
He added that the report should also be understood in the context of the US Supreme Court’s February ruling that unilateral tariff measures imposed by US President Donald Trump were unlawful. Rather than directly threatening higher tariffs, the investigation could give Washington an alternative legal and institutional basis for keeping existing tariffs in place while pressing Seoul to honour its commitments under the trade agreement reached last November.
Kim Kwang-suk, head of the economic research department at the Korea Economic and Industrial Research Institute, said Washington appeared to be using allegations of overproduction to maintain high tariffs and pressure major trading partners into fulfilling existing investment pledges and making additional investments in the US.
“The Trump administration appears to have found a new rationale for its high-handed tariff policy by invoking concerns over excess production, potentially providing additional leverage to demand that trading partners deliver on existing investment promises – and commit to more than they have already pledged,” Kim said.
The USTR argued that South Korea’s manufacturing-oriented economic model relied excessively on expanding production capacity and exports rather than stimulating domestic consumption. It cited goods exports equivalent to 35.9 per cent of South Korea’s gross domestic product, compared with 7.1 per cent in the US, based on 2021–25 averages.
Particular scrutiny was directed at Seoul’s K-Semiconductor Belt strategy, introduced in 2021 with the aim of establishing the world’s largest semiconductor supply chain by 2030.
The report pointed to around US$530 billion in planned semiconductor investment over two decades, tax incentives of up to 50 per cent for research and development and 20 per cent for facility investment, as well as government support for electricity, water supplies and other infrastructure, alongside preferential financing for chipmakers.
It also highlighted the proposed semiconductor cluster in the Gwangju and Jeolla regions, backed by corporate investment commitments of around 800 trillion won (US$518 billion), and South Korea’s dominant position in the global memory chip market.
Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix together accounted for more than 70 per cent of global dynamic random-access memory (DRAM) production and 51 per cent of NAND flash production, according to the report.
Although semiconductor products were exempt from the proposed additional duties under the investigation, the sector’s domestic production and investment policies remained a central focus of Washington’s allegations.
A graduate student in semiconductor engineering at Korea University in Seoul in June. Photo: Reuters
South Korea rejected the characterisation of its industrial policies as contributing to structural overproduction, arguing that its support measures were designed to strengthen corporate innovation and provide infrastructure needed for industrial development rather than encourage state-led expansion regardless of market demand.
“Our industrial policies provide indirect support for corporate innovation and infrastructure in accordance with market principles. They are not designed to encourage state-led overproduction,” an industry ministry official said.
Seoul also received assurances from Washington that the final tariff rate would remain consistent with the bilateral trade agreement reached last year.
“During consultations ahead of the announcement, the US side confirmed that the final applicable tariff would honour the deal reached between the two countries,” the official told reporters in a background briefing on Wednesday.
The official said the assurance had been repeated through multiple channels, including at senior levels, and that Seoul would continue to press for the agreed tariff rate during subsequent consultations and hearings.
But analysts dismissed Washington’s allegations of semiconductor overcapacity, arguing that the industry was struggling to keep pace with rapidly growing global demand.
Hur said Seoul needed to make a stronger case that the semiconductor industry faced supply constraints rather than producing more than the market could absorb.
“The US appears to want South Korea to reduce semiconductor production at home and shift more manufacturing capacity to the United States,” he said, noting that Trump had threatened in January to impose 25 per cent tariffs over the construction of semiconductor plants in South Korea, and that similar arguments had now resurfaced in the latest investigation.
Kim said demand had recently outpaced supply, particularly in the memory chip sector, with DRAM prices surging severalfold as manufacturers struggled to produce enough chips to meet growing requirements.
For South Korea, the immediate priority should be to convince Washington that its semiconductor industry faced a global shortage of production capacity rather than generating excess supply, he said.
“If further investment commitments become necessary, Seoul should ensure that they are structured in ways that serve South Korea’s broader economic interests, rather than simply responding to American pressure,” he added.
By Park Chan-kyong

title_en: China’s giant sphere for hunting ghost particles has won a top engineering prize
content_en:
Supreme Award judges praised ‘exceptional collaboration’ behind Juno, which is buried deep underground in Guangdong province.
China’s Juno facility won the Supreme Award from the London-based Institution of Structural Engineers this month. Photo: Juno/Institute of High Energy Physics, Chinese Academy of Sciences
A giant transparent ball – as tall as a 12-storey building and buried 700 metres (2,300 feet) under the rolling hills of southern China to catch ghostly particles – has won one of the world’s top engineering prizes.
The Jiangmen Underground Neutrino Observatory, or Juno, took out the Supreme Award at a London ceremony on November 6 hosted by the Institution of Structural Engineers, the largest professional body in the field.
Designed by the Beijing Institute of Architectural Design and run by the Chinese Academy of Sciences, Juno features 20,000 tonnes of special liquid, a 40-metre steel frame and more than 40,000 sensors that watch for flashes of light set off by neutrinos from nearby nuclear plants.
Judges picked it as the best of nine winners, chosen from projects in 15 countries, pointing to the precision its builders had to achieve. They noted that the acrylic sphere had to stay strong as it was filled with liquid and needed to hold up to earthquakes deep underground.
“This extraordinary facility demonstrates the vital role of structural engineering in enabling world-leading scientific research,” the panel said.
They also praised the “exceptional collaboration between engineers, scientists and international partners” behind the project, which brings together researchers from 17 nations, including China and Britain.
Judges noted the precision the builders had to achieve at the facility, which began collecting data in 2025. Photo: Juno/Institute of High Energy Physics, Chinese Academy of Sciences
Neutrinos are among the most common particles in the universe, pouring out of the sun, distant stars and even the rocks beneath our feet. Trillions pass through our bodies every second, but they almost never hit anything.
In October, the Nobel Prize in Physics went to Francis Halzen of the University of Wisconsin-Madison for his leading role in building IceCube, an observatory that uses a cubic kilometre of ice at the South Pole to catch neutrinos from deep space.
Juno aims to solve a decades-old puzzle: which of the three types of neutrino is the heaviest. The answer could help explain where these particles get their mass, and why matter won out over antimatter after the big bang, leaving a universe of something rather than nothing.
First proposed in 2008, the 2.7 billion yuan (US$404.8 million) project broke ground in 2015 and began collecting data in 2025. It is the first of three next-generation neutrino detectors to start work, as Japan’s Hyper-Kamiokande and the US Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment are still to be completed.
[embedded media]
Building it was no easy job. Groundwater gushing through cracks in the rock forced crews to pump out 12,000 tonnes a day and move the main hall 35 metres higher, delaying the project by about four years, according to the Institute of High Energy Physics which leads Juno.
Workers then bonded more than 260 acrylic panels into a ball nearly three times as wide as the previous record holder. Its 12cm (4.7-inch) wall is, for its size, as thin as an eggshell.
During filling, liquid levels inside and outside the shell were kept within a few centimetres of each other. The finished sphere came out only about a centimetre off its designed size, the institute said.
The Institution of Structural Engineers founded the Structural Awards in 1968, and the Supreme Award was introduced in 2003. The awards have honoured landmark projects such as the Sydney Opera House and the Centre Pompidou in Paris. Chinese projects have taken the top prize before, including the Tibetan Art Museum, transformed by Tongji Architectural Design, in 2024.
By Ling Xin

title_en: Philippines’ Sara Duterte says she does not expect fair ICC trial for her father
content_en:
The Philippine vice-president believes that the court will want to ‘make a statement’ out of Rodrigo Duterte’s coming trial.
Philippine Vice President Sara Duterte gestures as she answers questions during a news conference at her office in Manila on Friday. Photo: AP
Philippine Vice-President Sara Duterte-Carpio said on Friday she did not expect a fair hearing when her ex-president father’s crimes against humanity trial opened next week, predicting the under-fire International Criminal Court (ICC) would look to “make a statement”.
Duterte said “China, Russia and our BFF the United States” – an acronym for “best friend forever”, in a swipe at the Philippines’ close US ties under President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr – all considered the ICC a “political organisation” rather than an impartial arbiter.
Last month, the United States announced sanctions aimed at crippling the court’s day-to-day operations, with Trump vowing to dismantle it “brick by brick” over its warrant for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for alleged crimes in Gaza.
Rodrigo Duterte, 81, has been held in detention at The Hague since his arrest on an ICC warrant in March 2025 and is scheduled to enter a plea on Monday over drug war killings that took place between 2011 and 2019.
Former Philippine president Rodrigo Duterte appears at the ICC in The Hague during a preparatory session on September 16. Photo: AFP
“We don’t expect a fair trial from the ICC,” his daughter told reporters on Friday.
“I think the ICC, after the ganging up of superpowers, [will] want to make a statement that they are in the right. So there is no one else there that they would like to make a statement to. And that’s the case of Rodrigo Duterte,” she said.
She also referred to the case against her father as the “only” one facing the tribunal, an assertion she has made numerous times despite the fact that multiple suits in various stages of litigation are working their way through the ICC.
Duterte-Carpio added that she believed the case against her father and her own ongoing impeachment were aimed at keeping her off the board for the 2028 presidential election.
She was impeached by the House of Representatives in May and is currently on trial in the Senate, where a guilty verdict would see her barred permanently from elected office.
“I still believe that it’s about the 2028 elections, whether there will be elections or there will be no elections. It’s about the change of leadership, if there will ever be a change of leadership,” she told reporters, without naming her arch-rival, Marcos.
Supporters of the elder Duterte believe he was “kidnapped” and sent to The Hague due to his daughter’s spectacular falling-out with the man she once swept to power with in a landslide 2022 election victory.
While praising the “Dutch prison’s” treatment of her father, Duterte-Carpio on Friday once again called for him to be allowed to witness the proceedings remotely.
“I think it’s unfair that they are demanding that he attend the trial, every day … because of his age. He cannot sit eight hours a day on his chair. And I don’t think he can focus his time and attention … to something for eight hours,” she said.
“It’s unfair to demand that of an 81-year-old man.”
Llore Pasco, a mother of two victims of alleged extra judicial killings during former Philippine president Rodrigo Duterte’s so called war on drugs, heads to The Hague on Thursday to observe Duterte’s ICC trial at the ICC. Photo: AP
Despite his lawyers arguing that Duterte was unfit to stand trial because of cognitive decline, judges ordered him to stand trial and attend hearings. Court sessions will be shortened to accommodate his age.
During the trial, which is expected to run well into 2027, more than 500 alleged victims will be represented in court.
Llore Pasco, a mother who lost her two sons, is travelling to The Hague to attend the trial that will open on her 73rd birthday. She said she had ⁠never imagined she would see Duterte in the dock.
“This is the greatest and most beautiful gift you could give me,” she said hours before boarding a plane to the Netherlands.
“My only wish ‌is not just justice for my children but for all those killed during the time of Rodrigo Duterte. I hope the killings stop for the next generation.”
Additional reporting by Reuters
By Agence France-Presse

title_en: China and India hold fresh border talks as both boost military readiness before winter
content_en:
India concludes 9-day northern airforce drills while PLA plateau units upgrade winter medical and food supplies.
Beijing and New Delhi have concluded talks regarding the China-India border region. They were described as “cordial” while China’s foreign ministry says the border area is “generally stable”. Photo: Indian Ministry of Defence/AFP
China and India have held talks to manage tensions over their hotly contested frontier, even as both ramp up combat readiness and logistical support.
They remained in contact through diplomatic and military channels to keep peace along the border, China’s defence ministry said on Thursday.
“Currently, the China-India border area remains generally stable, with both sides maintaining communication through diplomatic and military channels – such as corps-commander-level talks – to jointly implement the consensus reached by both parties and safeguard peace and tranquillity in the border region,” ministry spokesman Chen Xi said.
The two sides concluded their fresh round of talks between military commanders in the eastern sector of the Line of Actual Control (LAC), the de facto border. The first such talks in the region took place in September.
The meeting began on November 8 and ran for nearly 10 days with a short break, according to The Indian Express. Described as “cordial”, the talks sought to establish rules of engagement, avoid friction among frontline troops, maintain open communication channels and ease tensions before winter, the report said.
[embedded media]
Beijing does not recognise the Indian-controlled state of Arunachal Pradesh, which China calls Zangnan or Southern Tibet, and claims as part of the Tibet autonomous region.
Neither side has issued an official statement on the meeting.
The eastern sector of the China-India border has seen heightened tensions in recent months amid reports of confrontations and stand-offs. In October, India’s Indo-Tibetan Border Police said confrontations with Chinese troops were “continuing at multiple locations along the Arunachal Pradesh border”.
Meanwhile, both neighbours have continued to bolster their combat readiness and logistical support.
Last week, India wrapped up a nine-day airforce exercise in its northern part near the border with China, during which it flew Rafale and Su-30MKI fighter jets, two mainstays of its military capable of operating in harsh terrain.
The Indian Air Force is also expected to receive its first domestically built C-295 aircraft by the end of this year. Designed to carry troops, equipment and supplies, the aircraft will reportedly boost the air force’s tactical transport and logistics capabilities and support operations in difficult terrain near the border.

title_en: Failed California billionaire tax proposal gets close look in China tax circles
content_en:
A former senior official warns that unilateral levies on the rich can backfire, as Beijing steps up efforts to widen its own tax net.
California Governor Gavin Newsom is among those who opposed California’s Proposition 40, the billionaire tax proposal that was narrowly voted down this month. Photo: TNS
The failure of a billionaire tax proposal in California is drawing attention in Chinese tax circles, with a former senior tax official dissecting the vote and implications in a state-run newspaper as Beijing steps up its own scrutiny of the super-rich.
Zhang Zhiyong, a former deputy head of the State Taxation Administration (STA), said the taxation of existing wealth was now a “mandatory” issue rather than “optional”, as AI had profoundly transformed global wealth concentration patterns.
“The value of the California case lies in helping people see the necessary conditions for levying a wealth tax,” he wrote in a commentary published this week in China Taxation News, a publication supervised by the STA.
California voters rejected Proposition 40 this month, with 52 per cent voting against it. The measure would have imposed a one-off 5 per cent tax on the accumulated wealth of the state’s billionaires, primarily to fund healthcare.
Healthcare workers rallied in Sacramento in August in support of California’s Proposition 40, which would have imposed a one-time tax on the state’s billionaires. Photo: TNS
Opponents, backed by US$378 million in donations from the super-rich, argued that the tax would drive wealthy residents out of the state and erode its tax base. Governor Gavin Newsom was among them.
Zhang said the mobility of people and assets made it risky for a single state to levy such a tax on its own. “Unilateral and hasty action often proves counterproductive,” he wrote.
The commentary did not refer to China’s own tax policies.
However, it came as Beijing widens its tax net and steps up enforcement on wealthy individuals.
Taxpayers have declared more than 160 billion yuan (US$24 billion) in personal income tax on offshore trust income since Beijing introduced new rules in late July, official data shows. More than 120 billion yuan was collected in October alone, helping lift national personal income tax receipts that month by almost 90 per cent year on year. The rules impose a 20 per cent tax on income and gains from such trusts.
The offshore trust levy may not mark the end of Beijing’s drive to widen its tax net.
Bank of America analysts have said enforcement could eventually extend to overseas employment income. In September, authorities scrapped a tax exemption on dividends and bonuses received by foreign individuals from foreign-invested firms, in place since 1994.
Recent legislative recommendations have also revived debate over a long-awaited inheritance tax.
Zhang listed other hurdles to levying a wealth tax, including how to value private assets and coordinate across borders. He noted that wealth was already taxed in part through levies on income, capital gains and wealth transfers.
“Future global tax reform, including wealth taxes, still depends heavily on inclusive multilateral consensus, effective rule-making and enforcement cooperation based on information sharing,” Zhang wrote.
By Daisy Wu

title_en: Why Trump’s new tariff threats may spur Southeast Asia to rethink US trade deals
content_en:
The six Southeast Asian countries at risk of facing higher US tariffs may face a backlash if they concede too much to Trump, analysts say.
A 3D-printed miniature model of US President Donald Trump alongside the word “tariffs”. Photo: Reuters
US President Donald Trump’s latest tariff threats have led analysts to question whether the trade deals Southeast Asian countries previously struck with Washington were worth pursuing, as those countries consider further talks with his administration.
On Wednesday, US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer announced proposed tariffs on imports from 14 major trading partners: China, the European Union, Switzerland, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, Bangladesh and India, plus Singapore, Vietnam, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Cambodia.
The duties stem from investigations under Section 301 of US trade law into excess capacity, meaning the ability to produce more goods than market demand warrants. The investigations began in March this year, after the Supreme Court struck down Trump’s previously announced tariffs.
China faces proposed US tariffs of up to 20 per cent under the current trade truce – rising to as much as 40 per cent if the truce is not extended – while Vietnam is looking at possible levies of up to 35 per cent, the highest among the six Southeast Asian economies targeted.
Greer said the latest tariffs would “level the playing field for American workers and chart a new, more sustainable course for the world economy”.
The proposal came just days after Trump attended the Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit in Manila and the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen.
Robert Walker, a research fellow at the Lowy Institute’s Indo-Pacific Development Centre, said the tariffs were unlikely to be related to those trips and were probably tied to the 301 investigations.
“The act of imposing more tariffs targeting allies, trade partners and competitors is hard to reconcile with strategic motivations at this point,” he said.
A cargo ship seen docked at Pasir Panjang port terminal in Singapore. The city state said on Thursday that it was “very disappointed” with proposed new US tariffs on its exports. Photo: AFP
Walker added that the proposed duties would bring overall tariff rates close to their levels before the US Supreme Court ruling.
“It is reverting tariff levels roughly to those previously negotiated last year and should be seen as a continuation of Trump’s efforts to impose tariffs on trading partners,” he added.
Malaysia, Indonesia and Cambodia have signed so-called agreements on reciprocal trade (ARTs) with the US. Trade talks between Thailand and the Trump administration are at an advanced stage, while Singapore and Vietnam are still negotiating. Under the deals, the US promises to lower tariffs in exchange for concessions, such as market access and digital regulations, from Southeast Asian partners.
Jaideep Singh, an analyst at the Institute of Strategic and International Studies in Malaysia, said Washington’s announcement marked a return to the baseline tariff rate of around 18 to 20 per cent last seen in late 2025.
Kevin Chen, an associate research fellow at the S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies, said the proposed levies had been anticipated since the US Trade Representative’s investigations ended in May. He attributed the delay to the US midterm elections and the Asean and Apec summits in November.
“Rather than a coherent strategy, it would be more accurate to say that the Trump administration aims to force countries to conclude ARTs with favourable terms for the US,” he said.
Ahmed Albayrak, a research associate at the Lowy Institute, said Washington clearly wanted to speed up negotiations with its Southeast Asian and other partners. He said Trump hoped to secure deals before the US-China trade truce ended.
Sellers wait for customers at a clothes market in Banda Aceh, Indonesia. The US is proposing new import tariffs of up to 18 per cent on Indonesian goods. Photo: EPA
Singh said that, despite the US Supreme Court ruling, Trump still retained considerable executive power to advance an “increasingly protectionist” trade policy.
“By this point, exporters and governments have become socialised to the notion that the tariffs will stay in some form or another for the remainder of Trump’s term, even if the legal basis or exact instrument may change,” he said.
The Office of the United States Trade Representative will begin public hearings on the proposed tariffs on January 25. They cannot take effect until the process concludes.
“Countries that have signed ARTs will now have another data point to assess whether the agreements were worth their price. Countries that are still negotiating with the US can assess how their neighbours fared,” Chen said.
Cambodia, Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand could face tariffs of up to 18 per cent on their exports, compared with 10 to 12.5 per cent levies on many goods now. Singapore’s could reach 20 per cent, against the 12.5 per cent rate imposed since July. Vietnam could face up to 35 per cent, or 20 per cent if it reaches a trade deal with Washington, compared with 12.5 per cent on many goods currently.
Albayrak said several trade partners were wary of making sweeping concessions because of potential domestic backlash.
“Some of these countries, like Indonesia and Malaysia, were criticised for giving up sovereignty, but at the time I don’t think people expected the tariffs to change so often in the period since,” he said. “For now, early movers seem to be enjoying lower rates, but as with every tariff announcement, the rates are not final.”
[embedded media]
Chen warned of the potential “extraordinary cost” to Southeast Asian economies from their trade deals with Trump, citing commitments to buy billions of dollars’ worth of US goods and concessions on digital policy positions.
Given the latest tariff proposals, regional governments must be asking whether signing a trade deal with Washington was ultimately worth it, he said.
Walker predicted that the US’ attempts to “manage trade” would likely be unsuccessful.
“Therefore many governments are likely hoping to ride out the next two years of the Trump administration and then renege on promises and commitments where possible,” he said.
By Sam Beltran

title_en: Hong Kong Science Park veteran named CEO of Hung Shui Kiu industrial park operator
content_en:
Yiu Hing-leung will assume office on December 1 for three-year term, tasked with attracting high-value-added industries to Northern Metropolis.
Yiu Hing-leung has more than 30 years of experience in the technology and industrial sectors. Photo: Handout
A former senior executive of the Hong Kong Science and Technology Parks Corporation (HKSTP) has been appointed CEO of the Hung Shui Kiu Industry Park Company to accelerate the development of the Northern Metropolis megaproject.
The park company, the first government-owned entity established to drive the megaproject’s development, said on Friday that Yiu Hing-leung would assume office on December 1 for a three-year term.
Yiu has more than 30 years of experience in the technology and industrial sectors. He previously served at HKSTP, where he held several key leadership positions, including chief corporate development officer and head of innofacturing.
Before that, Yiu also took up senior executive roles at a technology start-up and a multinational corporation.
Yiu was chosen by a selection panel led by Financial Secretary Paul Chan Mo-po in an open recruitment exercise launched by the government earlier.
The park company’s chairman, Jeffrey Lam Kin-fung, said Yiu would spearhead the park in attracting a high-value-added and diverse range of industries to set up operations in the long term.
“Expediting the development of the Northern Metropolis is one of the major objectives of Hong Kong’s first five-year plan. The establishment of the wholly government-owned Park Company is a crucial instrument for the government to drive industry development in the Northern Metropolis through diversified approaches,” he said.
Under the Northern Metropolis scheme, 30,000 hectares (74,132 acres) of land near the border with mainland China will be transformed into an engine for economic growth and a housing hub.
The park company is responsible for the development and operation of the 27.5-hectare Hung Shui Kiu Industry Park, which will drive the development of industries including high-value-added and smart production, such as pharmaceutical manufacturing and food processing.
By Cannix Yau

title_en: Zelensky says Trump calling Putin ‘my friend’ is like being buddies with Hitler in WWII
content_en:
The Russian president cannot be a friend as he is an aggressor and killer, the Ukrainian leader says.
Russia’s President Vladimir Putin (right) and US President Donald Trump shake hands during a meeting on the sidelines of the Apec summit in Shenzhen on November 19. Photo: Sputnik / Reuters
Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelensky said US ⁠President Donald ⁠Trump calling Russia’s ⁠Vladimir Putin “my friend” was strange and akin to making the same comment about Adolf Hitler during World War II.
In an interview ‌with the BBC, the Ukrainian president said it was up to Trump what he said or posted but he called it “strange” to call Putin a friend.
“He’s an aggressor … and a killer. He can’t be ⁠a friend,” he said, speaking in English. “It’s the same that ‌somebody says about Hitler during the second world war that he’s a good friend. ‌No, he’s not a friend.”
Zelensky was speaking a week ⁠after ⁠Trump had embraced Putin as a “friend” at a summit in China. Days ‌later, Trump posted a photo on his Truth Social platform of the ‌pair ‌shaking hands there and titled it “My Friend”.
Trump’s relationship with ‌Zelensky has long been uneasy, most memorably breaking down ⁠publicly in February 2025 when the US president rebuked him ⁠in the Oval Office.
US President Donald Trump (right) clashes with Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky in the Oval Office of the White House on February 28, 2025. Photo: AFP
More recently, the pair have clashed as Trump blamed Ukrainian strikes on ‌Russian refineries for ‌high energy costs and threatened to cut off intelligence support, while Zelensky has said Trump’s position is encouraging Russia to continue attacks on Ukraine.
Trump on Thursday said he was unsure if Putin would attend the coming G20 summit in Miami but he would “like to have” him there.
Trump’s invitation to Putin to attend the G20 was made in September but remains unanswered less than a month before it is set to begin in mid-December.
“I don’t know, but if he wanted to come, he certainly can,” Trump told reporters at his Mar-a-Lago estate in Florida. “If it ‌were up to me, I’d like to have him.”
Putin has been a pariah on the international stage since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in early 2022, and Washington’s traditional European allies have questioned his G20 invitation.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has pushed for Zelensky to be invited, on the presumption that Putin’s presence would be to discuss the war’s fate.
The United States is yet to broker a deal to end the war, with Trump insisting he is working with both sides to stop the fighting.

In an interview ‌with the BBC, the Ukrainian president said it was up to Trump what he said or posted but he called it “strange” to call Putin a friend.
“He’s an aggressor … and a killer. He can’t be ⁠a friend,” he said, speaking in English. “It’s the same that ‌somebody says about Hitler during the second world war that he’s a good friend. ‌No, he’s not a friend.”
Zelensky was speaking a week ⁠after ⁠Trump had embraced Putin as a “friend” at a summit in China. Days ‌later, Trump posted a photo on his Truth Social platform of the ‌pair ‌shaking hands there and titled it “My Friend”.
Trump’s relationship with ‌Zelensky has long been uneasy, most memorably breaking down ⁠publicly in February 2025 when the US president rebuked him ⁠in the Oval Office.

Trump on Thursday said he was unsure if Putin would attend the coming G20 summit in Miami but he would “like to have” him there.
Trump’s invitation to Putin to attend the G20 was made in September but remains unanswered less than a month before it is set to begin in mid-December.
“I don’t know, but if he wanted to come, he certainly can,” Trump told reporters at his Mar-a-Lago estate in Florida. “If it ‌were up to me, I’d like to have him.”
Putin has been a pariah on the international stage since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in early 2022, and Washington’s traditional European allies have questioned his G20 invitation.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has pushed for Zelensky to be invited, on the presumption that Putin’s presence would be to discuss the war’s fate.
The United States is yet to broker a deal to end the war, with Trump insisting he is working with both sides to stop the fighting.

title_en: Will exit of key executive cloud WuXi Biologics’ US outlook?
content_en:
Analysts remain confident in the Chinese biotech services giant’s US business despite speculation over growing geopolitical pressure.
WuXi Biologics maintains a large footprint in the US, with North America contributing more than 58 per cent of revenue in 2025. Photo: Shutterstock
The planned departure of a top executive at WuXi Biologics’ US arm has sparked debate over the geopolitical pressures facing the Chinese biotech services giant, although analysts remain upbeat about the company’s outlook in the American market.
Nuno Fontes, president of WuXi Biologics’ US subsidiary, said in a LinkedIn post on Thursday that he was leaving the company, calling it “a difficult personal decision” driven by family considerations.
While lauding the Chinese firm as the “best global CDMO” – or contract development and manufacturing organisation – with a “very bright” future, Fontes said he had accepted a new leadership role “closer to home” with a US-based company. His last day at WuXi Biologics is on Monday.
Some industry observers in China have linked Fontes’ departure in part to Washington’s heightened scrutiny of cross-border biotech collaboration.
WuXi Biologics’ operations were being “placed under a microscope” amid the “lingering fallout” from the Biosecure Act and a growing US push to localise supply chains, Chinese industry outlet Guide View wrote in a commentary on Friday following the announcement.
The Biosecure Act, signed into law last December, seeks to restrict federal funding and contracts involving “biotechnology companies of concern”, with an initial list of designated firms expected to be released next month.
WuXi Biologics did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Analysts played down concerns about Fontes’ departure. Recent developments suggested a “more constructive backdrop rather than escalating geopolitical pressure”, said Cui Cui, head of Asia healthcare research at investment bank Jefferies.
Earlier this month, WuXi AppTec, WuXi Biologics’ sister company focused on small-molecule drugs instead of biologics, was removed from a Pentagon blacklist of entities allegedly linked to the Chinese military. Analysts described the move as significantly positive for both the firm and the sector.
“We do not expect his departure to have a material impact on the company’s US operations,” Cui said, adding that Jefferies remained confident about WuXi Biologics’ fundamentals and expected growth to accelerate.
WuXi Biologics maintains a large footprint in the US. North America contributed 58.1 per cent of revenue in 2025, up from 57.3 per cent in 2024, according to its latest annual report. Europe and China, its second- and third-largest markets, contributed 23.1 per cent and 12.3 per cent of revenue, respectively.
The company said earlier this week that it was continuing to expand its US presence after its facility in Cranbury, New Jersey, became ready for commercial production of complex biologics following the completion of a key test.
John Yung, head of Asia healthcare research at investment bank Citi, also struck a positive note this week.
While artificial intelligence-designed drugs were unlikely to outperform existing treatments before 2030, Yung said the commitment of frontier AI firms to drug discovery should benefit laboratory service providers such as WuXi Biologics.
WuXi Biologics’ Hong Kong-listed shares closed 7.16 per cent higher on Friday after rising 1.43 per cent on Thursday.
By Xinmei Shen

title_en: EU seeks bigger Indian Ocean security role without rattling India
content_en:
Landmark EU talks with the Indian Ocean Rim Association could offer smaller states new defence partners, analysts say.
Attendees at the first high-level maritime security talks between the EU and the Indian Ocean Rim Association in New Delhi on Tuesday. Photo: EU
The European Union’s push to strengthen its security role in the Indian Ocean could give smaller countries more options for defence partnerships, but analysts say Brussels will need to navigate India’s desire to preserve its regional leadership and strategic autonomy.
The first high-level maritime security talks between the EU and the Indian Ocean Rim Association (IORA), held in New Delhi on Tuesday, underlined Europe’s growing interest in a region where China and the US are competing for influence.
The agenda looked beyond piracy and maritime trafficking to newer threats, including shadow fleets and the security of undersea cables and other critical infrastructure.
IORA, founded in 1997, has 23 members across Asia, Africa and Australia and 12 dialogue partners, including China and the US. India is the current chair. The association provides a platform for promoting regional economic integration and cooperation on maritime security, disaster management, fisheries and tourism, among other areas.
Jean-Eric Paquet, the EU’s ambassador to India, stressed the need for coordinated international action on emerging maritime security challenges.
“The message from the EU is clear, as set out in the EU Indo-Pacific Strategy and in the Strategic Compass, we are committed to strengthening security and defence cooperation with partners in the region,” Paquet said at the talks on Tuesday.
He said both the EU and IORA had identified maritime security as a priority, with particular emphasis on regional cooperation and information sharing. The EU, he added, had direct interest in the security of sea lanes of communication.
Jean-Eric Paquet, the EU’s ambassador to India. He said the bloc was committed to strengthening security and defence cooperation with the Indian Ocean region. Photo: EU
The round table also gave updates on EU Naval Force Operation Atalanta, which helps secure the western Indian Ocean and the Red Sea.
The EU has been an IORA dialogue partner since October 2023. Among EU member states, France is a full IORA member, while Germany and Italy are dialogue partners.
The talks come as India has deepened its security and defence ties with the EU. In January, the two sides signed a security and defence partnership covering maritime security, defence industry and technology, cybersecurity, hybrid threats, space and counterterrorism.
Dr Shubhamitra Das, an associate professor at Jawaharlal Nehru University’s Centre for Indo-Pacific Studies, said the EU’s Indo-Pacific strategy was mainly driven by a wish to work with Indian Ocean states to ensure freedom of navigation and respect for international law.
“The EU focuses on maritime security and regional cooperation, and can contribute more to building resilience structures for institutional development and organisational skills,” she said.
Das said IORA’s geographical reach could be leveraged to strengthen institutional cooperation across the Indo-Pacific and welcomed the talks, noting that the association had yet to live up to its potential.
“The Indian Ocean is a vibrant region with significant trade routes that have become geopolitically crucial and, on the other hand, piracy, drugs, arms and human trafficking, cybersecurity, grey-zone activities are undermining maritime security and destabilising the equilibrium,” she said.
‘An added advantage’
India had strong relations with many European countries and as IORA chair its priority was regional cooperation, Das said.
“India, Indonesia, Australia, Kenya, Saudi Arabia, Sri Lanka and other stakeholders can play a significant role in improving and increasing the workability of IORA,” she said. “The EU’s presence will be an added advantage, especially due to the unpredictability of the US’ presence and strategy in the Indo-Pacific region.”
Smaller countries had shown their agency in multilateral forums and were wary of new entrants, Das said. “But IORA is a multilateral organisation, and the EU is the first intergovernmental union of 27 European states; becoming a dialogue partner is the right approach for international cooperation,” she said.
“The present arrangement in IORA and the EU builds a new platform where issues of importance can be discussed, while the major concern of small countries is to let the multilateral organisations work along with international cooperation and international law that will give them both recognition and the most deserved voice.”
Attendees at the maritime security talks between the EU and the Indian Ocean Rim Association in New Delhi on Tuesday. Photo: EU
A third option
Dongkeun Lee, a policy fellow at the Asia-Pacific Leadership Network specialising in maritime security, said the EU must step up diplomatic engagement to safeguard its sea lines of communication as it expanded its Indian Ocean presence.
India would welcome European engagement, Lee said, provided Europe did not try to undermine Delhi’s leadership role in the Indian Ocean.
“Interest in the Indian Ocean from external powers is not a new phenomenon. During the Cold War, both the Soviet Union and the US expressed interest in the region, but India consistently maintained its strategic autonomy there,” he said, adding that Brussels should respect India’s role as regional leader.
Small powers, however, are likely to view new extra-regional players as an opportunity, according to Lee.
“This means that rather than being limited to choosing between existing great powers, small powers could enjoy greater opportunities to choose their external security partners,” he said.
But that might not appeal to all countries, Lee said. “Countries that have already sided with one power may perceive the introduction of new players into the region as simply destabilising the region by adding another uncontrollable variable.”
Nilanthi Samaranayake, a security analyst and adjunct fellow at the East-West Centre in Washington, said IORA was arguably the most successful regional institution spanning the Indian Ocean and it was no surprise that the EU wanted to deepen ties.
“In particular, the EU member states have clear interests in ensuring the preservation of fish stocks and sustainable fishing practices in the Indian Ocean,” she said.
“Smaller Indian Ocean countries generally seek as many partners as possible to help meet their development objectives. As a result, the EU’s growing interest in the region’s economic and marine ecological future is of direct relevance to them.”
By Junaid Kathju

title_en: Third Trump-branded project takes shape in Hanoi amid US-Vietnam tariff talks
content_en:
Government officials met the Trump Organisation’s partners shortly after the US announced possible new tariffs ‌on Vietnam.
Eric Trump (right), son of US President Donald Trump, and wife Lara (second left) take a selfie with attendees of the groundbreaking ceremony for the Trump International Hung Yen resort and golf course project in Vietnam on May 21, 2025. Photo: AFP
Vietnamese ⁠business partners of the ⁠Trump Organisation are planning ⁠a skyscraper in Hanoi, three people with knowledge of the new project said.
It is one of three Trump-branded projects in the works in the Southeast Asian nation. A US$1.5 billion ‌Trump-branded golf complex is being developed near Hanoi by local partners of the Trump Organisation. A separate Trump Tower is planned in Ho Chi Minh City, people involved with the project have said.
All the projects were being developed at no cost to the Trump Organisation, ⁠which earned money from the use of its brand, operating fees and property ‌sales, one person with direct knowledge of the plans said.
Vietnamese government officials met the Trump Organisation’s partners, which include ‌Kinh Bac City Development Holding, on Thursday to discuss the ⁠Hanoi project, ⁠according to two of the sources.
Demonstrators walk past the Trump Tower in Chicago as they take part in a “No Kings” protest against US President Donald Trump’s administration policies on March 28. Photo: Reuters
The meeting took place shortly after Washington announced possible new tariffs ‌of up to 35 per cent on Vietnam, which could be cut to 20 per cent if a trade ‌deal was ‌struck, they said.
One of the people said the project was ‌first submitted to the government in May and that it had not ⁠yet received approval.
All sources declined to be named as the information was ⁠not public. The plans for a new Trump Tower in Hanoi are being reported here for the first time.
The Trump Organisation, ‌US President Donald Trump’s ‌family business, was not immediately available for comment outside US working hours. Vietnam’s government and Kinh Bac City Development did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
The Trump Organisation is run by Trump’s sons, Eric and Donald Jnr, who are executive vice ⁠presidents. The White House has said that the president, upon taking office, ended his involvement in his businesses after placing them in a ⁠trust managed by his children.
Two of the sources said the Hanoi Trump Tower would be built on the western fringe of West Lake, an affluent area of the capital where foreign executives and diplomats live.
Pending approvals, construction could begin toward the ‌end of 2027 or in 2028, one ‌person said, adding that the plan submitted to authorities was for a building of at least 60 floors at an estimated cost of around US$1 billion.
Deal close
Vietnam’s Prime Minister Le Minh Hung said on ‌Friday that a trade deal was close as Hanoi had made strong commitments to the United States aimed at avoiding ⁠high tariffs that could ⁠hurt its export-reliant economy.
Industry officials, who expect an agreement in December, when Vietnam leader To Lam attends ⁠a G20 summit in Florida, see the new tariff threat as an inducement to reach a deal.
“I would not rule out a deal over the coming months,” ‌said Bruno Jaspaert, the head of DEEP C Industrial Zones, a network of industrial estates in northern Vietnam hosting export-oriented factories run by multinational companies.
A Samsung Electronics factory in Bac Ninh province, Vietnam, is seen on April 3, 2025. Photo: Reuters
Vietnam also faces a US investigation into ⁠accusations of intellectual property violations, with a February 28 deadline. Washington has also accused it of functioning as a transit point for Chinese goods headed to the United States.
The accusation is particularly ominous for Vietnam’s electronics industry, which uses large volumes of Chinese-made components to assemble devices such ‌as computers, tablets and video game consoles.
Samsung and ‌Tesla were among the companies that urged the US government not to increase tariffs on Vietnam over intellectual property, arguing that would hurt supply chains.

title_en: China’s Tencent makes AI drug discovery breakthrough with Nature paper
content_en:
Chinese tech giant is using AI to design novel treatments for obesity, diabetes and cancer.
Chinese tech giant Tencent Holdings is pushing to accelerate research using AI in drug discovery. Photo: Shutterstock
Tencent Holdings has published a paper on using artificial intelligence to automate drug discovery in the leading science journal Nature, marking a breakthrough for the Chinese tech giant as it accelerates AI-enabled scientific research.
The paper, submitted to the British journal in June 2025 but published on Wednesday, outlines the Shenzhen-based company’s efforts to design novel treatments for obesity, diabetes and cancer with the help of AI.
According to the paper, researchers from Tencent’s AI for Life Sciences Lab led development of ORIDTP, a platform for designing peptides that act on two therapeutic targets at once, an approach Tencent says could reduce the amount of laboratory screening needed to identify promising drug candidates.
“This shifts the traditional approach of screening large molecular libraries towards AI-driven, targeted optimisation of small batches of candidate peptides,” Tencent said in a post on the social platform WeChat on Thursday.
The findings were validated in preclinical trials on mice, with human clinical trials yet to be conducted. Researchers from eight other institutions were involved in the project, including the Chengdu University of Traditional Chinese Medicine, Xian Children’s Hospital and Monash University in Australia.
Tencent has expanded its push into AI-enabled scientific research in recent months. At an event in Hong Kong earlier this month, the company’s chief AI scientist, Vinces Yao Shunyu, outlined Tencent’s plans to automate drug discovery with AI, though he warned this must be done “with vigilance” to prevent harm to society.
AI has the potential to change what can be studied, who can study it, and at what scaleMoonshot AI
According to the paper, ORIDTP tackles a key challenge in drug discovery: how to design a single peptide that can hit two therapeutic targets simultaneously.
The researchers tested the platform in two areas of metabolic diseases and cancer immunotherapy. For obesity and diabetes, they found that the peptides activated both the GLP-1 receptor and the glucagon receptor, resulting in both weight loss and improved blood sugar control in the mice.
For cancer, the peptides targeted two immune checkpoints that help regulate immune responses, PD-1 and CTLA-4, resulting in a 94.2 per cent decrease in tumour volume compared with a control group.
In its WeChat post, Tencent said ORIDTP had been integrated into its flagship agentic AI product WorkBuddy.

title_en: Why did an AI chip frenzy send a Chinese blender maker’s stock soaring 370%?
content_en:
Investors mocked the firm’s high-speed blenders as ‘soy milk GPUs’ – grain processing units – while also speculating about ties to Huawei.
The Joyoung booth at the SNEIC Expo Centre in Shanghai, on March 12, 2026. Photo: NurPhoto via Getty Images
China’s artificial intelligence boom has sent retail investors scrambling for exposure to graphics processing units (GPUs) – even if it means settling for “grain processing units” instead.
Shares of Joyoung, a Chinese home appliance maker best known for its soy milk makers, surged to an all-time high of 45.54 yuan during Friday trading, extending a five-day winning streak. The Shenzhen-listed stock later gave back some of the gains to close 0.6 per cent higher at 42.15 yuan.
The rally caps an extraordinary run that has seen Joyoung’s shares nearly double over the past month and surge more than 370 per cent in six months, in contrast to a broader pullback in China’s tech sector as investors grow cautious over global AI valuations.
While genuine GPUs serve as the hardware backbone of China’s AI and semiconductor push, retail traders have playfully projected that enthusiasm onto Joyoung’s kitchen blenders.
Investors have flooded the company’s official investor relations platform with tongue-in-cheek inquiries about its “technological breakthroughs”. Mocking the firm’s high-speed blenders as “soy milk GPUs” capable of pulverising beans “down to the nanometre scale”, one user asked whether Joyoung could become “the first to achieve a 1-nanometre soybean node”.
A graphics processing unit (GPU) from Chinese chip company MetaX. Photo: Handout
Other online chatter went further, speculating about mass production of domestic lithography machines, ties to Huawei Technologies and space technology.
Joyoung – whose blenders, juicers and rice cookers are staples in Chinese households – has repeatedly tried to pour cold water on the hype. In responses on its investor platform, the company stressed that its appliances had nothing to do with chip manufacturing or processing nodes, denied any involvement in lithography machines, and urged retail traders to invest rationally.
In a Tuesday filing to the Shenzhen Stock Exchange – its sixth warning over “abnormal trading volatility” in two months – the Jinan, Shandong-based firm also sought to clarify its links to China’s tech and aerospace sectors.
While Joyoung holds a 7.92 per cent stake in Huawei-backed AI firm iDeepWise, it said it had no strategic partnership with the telecoms equipment giant and that the investment had no material impact on its core business.
Similarly, although its kitchenware is used on China’s space station, the company noted that the technology did not constitute a stand-alone business segment.
The speculative frenzy stands in stark contrast to Joyoung’s fundamentals. Third-quarter net profit attributable to shareholders fell 74.7 per cent year on year to 216,346 yuan (US$32,462), against a modest 2 per cent dip in revenue to 1.56 billion yuan.
Huachuang Securities analysts attributed the profit drop mainly to minority investors increasing their stake in a subsidiary, diverting a larger share of profits away from the parent firm. Rising costs of stainless steel and other raw materials also squeezed margins in the quarter, the brokerage said in an October note.
By Iris Deng
